items.label: section_header
items.text: REMINDER

items.label: text
items.text: Remember the charge on the oxide ion is O²- and the charge on an alkali metal ion is M*.

items.label: section_header
items.text: EXTENSION WORK

items.label: text
items.text: When the alkali metals react with air, other types of oxide can also be formed, called peroxides (M2O2) and superoxides (MO2). These all still contain the M+ ion, it is the oxygen bit which is different. Lithium can also form a nitride (Li3N).

items.label: section_header
items.text: REACTIONS OF THE ALKALI METALS WITH THE AIR

items.label: text
items.text: Lithium, sodium and potassium are all stored in oil because they react with the air. If we look at a piece of sodium which has been taken out of the oil, it usually has a crust on the outside. It is not shiny unless it has been freshly cut.

items.label: text
items.text: When the piece of sodium is cut, the fresh surface is shiny but it tarnishes rapidly as the freshly exposed sodium reacts with oxygen in the air. If we do the same with a piece of lithium it tarnishes more slowly because lithium reacts more slowly than sodium. A freshly cut piece of potassium tarnishes extremely rapidly, more quickly than sodium. In this way we can see again that potassium is more reactive than sodium, which is more reactive than lithium. In each case the metal reacts with oxygen in the air to form an oxide with the formula M2O.

items.label: text
items.text: If we heat each of the metals in the air using a Bunsen burner, we get a much more vigorous reaction and it is more difficult to see which metal is most reactive because all the reactions are so rapid.

items.label: text
items.text: Lithium burns with a red flame to form lithium oxide.

items.label: text
items.text: Sodium burns with a yellow flame to form sodium oxide.

items.label: text
items.text: Potassium burns with a lilac flame to form potassium oxide.

items.label: text
items.text: The equation for all these reactions is:

items.label: formula
items.text: 4 M ( s ) + O _ { 2 } ( g ) \rightarrow 2 M _ { 2 } O ( s )

items.label: text
items.text: In each case the product formed is a white powder – the alkali metal oxide.

items.label: section_header
items.text: COMPOUNDS OF THE ALKALI METALS

items.label: text
items.text: All Group 1 metal ions are colourless. That means that their compounds will be colourless or white unless they are combinedwith a coloured negative ion. Potassium dichromate(Vl) is orange, for example, because the dichromate(Vl) ion is orange, and potassium manganate(VIl) is purple because the manganate(VIl)ion is purple. Group 1 compounds are typical ionic solids and are mostly soluble in water.

items.label: section_header
items.text: SUMMARISING THE MAIN FEATURES OF THE GROUP 1 ELEMENTS

items.label: text
items.text: Group 1 elements:

items.label: list_item
items.text: are metals

items.label: list_item
items.text: are soft with melting points and densities which are very low for metals

items.label: list_item
items.text: have to be stored out of contact with air or water

items.label: list_item
items.text: react rapidly with air to form coatings of the metal oxide

items.label: list_item
items.text: react with water to produce an alkaline solution of the metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas

items.label: list_item
items.text: increase in reactivity as you go down the group

items.label: list_item
items.text: form compounds in which the metal has a 1+ ion

items.label: list_item
items.text: have mainly white/colourless compounds which dissolve to produce colourless solutions.
